HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Outdoor Chores — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the outside jobs: the path, the plants, the leaves, the birds and the car — chores that wear costumes of play and work just as hard.

What is this?

Outdoor chores keep the home’s outside alive: sweep the path, water the plants, pick up the leaves, feed the birds, wash the car.

What does it mean?

Water is the hinge of this whole lesson: watering cans, buckets, sponges and hoses are chore tools and toy boxes at once. The work gets done because the water is wonderful.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a small watering can, a bucket with a sponge, and a patch of path or leaves. The birds need only a feeder or a sprinkle of seeds and some quiet.

Why this matters

Feeding the birds is the empathy chore: something alive depends on the showing up. And leaf-piles are the only chore with a built-in celebration clause — jump first, bag second.

What it teaches

Gross-motor work (sweeping, scrubbing circles), care for living things, and the outside-in rhythm of a job with a natural finish — the path is clean, the car is shiny.

Words to learn

sweep the pathwater the plantspick up leavesfeed the birdswash the car

Say this to your child

“"Outdoor chores! Sweep the path, water the plants, pile the leaves, feed the birds — and the car gets its bath. Everything outside drinks or shines today."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card outside: "five jobs — all of them better than inside jobs."
  2. Sweep the path together: long strokes, one direction, leaves gather like magic.
  3. Water the plants: glug, glug — one can, many pots, count as you go.
  4. Leaf pile: gather, jump (mandatory), then bag — celebration is part of the pipeline.
  5. Birds and car to close: seeds sprinkled quietly, then the bubbly circles on the car — the sponge and bucket finale.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Outdoor Chores" sit over five small scenes: a broom sweeping a path, a watering can over a potted plant, a rake and leaf pile, a birdhouse and bird by a feeder, and a soapy car mid-wash.

Ask your child

"Who do we feed in the morning?" (the birds) "What do the plants drink?" (water from the can) "Which chore lets you jump in the pile first?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might water the same plant until it swims, choreograph a leaf-pile jump routine, or stand sentry at the bird feeder shushing the whole street.

Out in the real world

The same five jobs exist at every grandparent’s and every holiday rental: paths, plants, birds, cars. A child with outdoor-chore skills is welcome everywhere.

Try it together

Water the Circuit: five cups of water, five thirsty things — a plant, the bird bath, the car’s one panel, the path’s one corner, the child’s own hands. The circuit runs until the cups are empty and the job is genuinely done.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do the plants drink from?" (the watering can) "What do the birds eat?" (the seeds) "What do we do before we bag the leaves?" (jump in the pile)

This lesson pairs with the Outdoor Chores flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.
